subject: english_literature
question_text: How do the heavens 'blaze forth' the death of Julius Caesar?
answer_text: Calpurnia sees ill-omens that predict the death of Caesar beforehand. The heavens predict the death of princes and great kings. She saw a lioness giving birth on the streets, fierce warriors fighting a bloody fight and blood falling on the Capitol, ghosts shrieking and squealing in the streets, the dead coming out of the grave. All these were unnatural happenings and indicated bad omen. Thus heavens “blaze forth” the death of Julius Caesar. All this signalled that someone as powerful as Caesar was bound to suffer.
final_answer: Thus, the unnatural occurrences signal the impending doom of Caesar.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires interpretation of symbolic events.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What does Calpurnia try to convince Caesar of?
answer_text: Calpurnia tries to convince Caesar of an ill-omen that she has seen her nightmares, which does mean a grave danger to Caesar’s life. She tries to convince Caesar not to go out as she fears he nightmares might turn true and Caesar might face danger for his life.
final_answer: Calpurnia fears for Caesar's life based on her ominous dreams.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character motivations.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Why does Calpurnia say Caesar's 'wisdom is consumed in confidence'? What does she mean?
answer_text: Calpurnia says that Caesar's 'wisdom is consumed in confidence' because Caesar decides to go to the Senate ignoring all the signs which foretell him about danger. Calpurnia felt that Caesar had become overconfident and because of this he couldn’t understand there was a threat to his life. Julius doesn’t act wise and declines the idea of staying back because if he did so, he would be considered a coward.
final_answer: Thus, Calpurnia believes Caesar's overconfidence blinds him to the dangers he faces.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character motivations and themes in the play.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What does Calpurnia dream about Caesar? How does Decius Brutus interpret the dream?
answer_text: Calpurnia dreamt that Caesar’s statue spouted blood from a hundred places and many Roman people came and washed their hands in it. Decius Brutus interprets it as a lucky and fortunate dream. He says that Rome and Romans will get a new life. Great man shall gather around Caesar and stain their handkerchief in his blood. Distinguished men will get honour at his hands and everything relating to him will be held in utmost reverence.
final_answer: Therefore, Decius Brutus twists the ominous dream into a positive omen for Caesar.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves interpretation of symbolism and character motivations.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What are the arguments put forward by Decius Brutus to convince Caesar to go to the Capitol?
answer_text: Decius Brutus, being a flatterer, interprets Calpurnia's dream as fair and fortunate one. Caesar's statue spouting blood from hundred places signifies his influence and reverence for him. He further says that the Senate has concluded to crown him. In case Caesar does not go to the Senate House that day, they may change their mind and he may miss such a golden opportunity to be the Roman king.
final_answer: Thus, Decius appeals to Caesar's ambition and pride to persuade him.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of persuasive techniques and character dynamics.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Why is Decius more successful than Calpurnia in persuading Caesar?
answer_text: Decius Brutus is a great flatterer. He is more successful in persuading Caesar than Calpurnia because his argument appeals to Caesar’s pride. While Calpurnia wishes that Caesar stay at home after seeing horrible dreams, Decius Brutus interprets the dreams as lucky and fortunate. According to him, they signify Caesar’s power and influence. He gives Caesar’s ego a boost. Caesar is totally carried away by his words and decides to go to the Capitol.
final_answer: Therefore, Decius's flattering approach effectively sways Caesar's decision.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires analysis of character motivations and persuasive strategies.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What is the petition put before Caesar by the conspirators? How does Caesar respond to it?
answer_text: The conspirators want that Caesar should call Publius Cimber home as he had banished him. They request him to review his earlier decision. However, Caesar is no mood to relent. He tells the conspirators that he is firm like a Pole Star. His heart will not be softened by bowing and stooping activities and if Mettellus Cimber continues such activities, he would turn him away like a street dog.
final_answer: Thus, Caesar's response reflects his steadfastness and refusal to be swayed.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of character traits and themes of power.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Who says 'Et tu Brute'? When are these words spoken? Why?
answer_text: Caesar utters these words which mean, 'You too, Brutus'. These are uttered when Brutus stabs Caesar and Caesar is too hurt to see that even his dear friend Brutus could resort to such treachery.
final_answer: Thus, these words signify Caesar's deep betrayal and shock.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of betrayal and character relationships.

subject: english_literature
question_text: In the moments following Caesar's death what do the conspirators proclaim to justify Caesar's death?
answer_text: After Caesar’s death, the conspirators claim that with Caesar’s death tyranny has ended in Rome. They shout slogans like ‘Peace, Liberty, Freedom and Enfranchisement’. They say that although Caesar was a great man, he had become too ambitious.
final_answer: Therefore, they justify the assassination as a necessary act for the greater good.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of political rhetoric and justification.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Seeing the body of Caesar, Antony is overcome by grief. What does he say about Caesar?
answer_text: Antony is overwhelmed with grief on seeing Caesar's dead body. He exclaims that inspite of Caesars' conquests, glories, triumphs and spoils, he lies so "low". He offers to be killed and lie by Caesar's side whom he calls the choice and master spirits of this age and "most noble".
final_answer: Thus, Antony expresses deep sorrow and admiration for Caesar despite his death.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character emotions and motivations.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Whom does Antony call 'the choice and master spirits of this age'? Why?
answer_text: Antony calls the conspirators “the choice and master spirits of this age”. He says this because they had just killed the leader of the Roman Empire.
final_answer: Therefore, Antony acknowledges the conspirators' significant action in Roman history.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of character perspectives and historical context.

subject: english_literature
question_text: How do Brutus and Cassius respond to Antony's speech?
answer_text: After listening to Antony's speech, Brutus assures him that even though the deed seems bloody, their intentions were worthy. Their pity for the common people of Rome overrode their pity for Caesar. Cassius offers Antony new position in the government.
final_answer: Thus, Brutus and Cassius justify their actions and seek to maintain their political stance.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires analysis of character motivations and political implications.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Why does Cassius object to allowing Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral? How does Brutus overcome this objection?
answer_text: Cassius does not think it would be proper Antony should speak at Caesar’s funeral as his speech may change the mind of the audience. But Brutus tells that Antony would only speak with their consent and he will speak first and his speech will enumerate reasons for Caesar’s death.
final_answer: Thus, Brutus reassures Cassius by asserting control over the situation.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of character dynamics and persuasive strategies.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What are the conditions imposed by the conspirators before allowing Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral?
answer_text: The conditions imposed on Mark Antony were that in his funeral speech he would not blame the conspirators, but speak all good things about Caesar. He had to speak from the same pulpit as Brutus and tell the people that he did so by the conspirators’ permission.
final_answer: Therefore, the conspirators sought to control the narrative surrounding Caesar's death.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of political strategy and speech dynamics.

subject: english_literature
question_text: When he is left alone with the body of Caesar what does Antony call Brutus and the others?
answer_text: Antony curses the murderers and he seeks forgiveness for being polite to them. He calls them ‘butchers’ who killed the noblest of men.
final_answer: Thus, Antony expresses his anger and betrayal towards the conspirators.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of character emotions and betrayal.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What prediction does Antony make regarding the future events in Rome?
answer_text: Antony prophesies that Italy will be ravaged with civil war, violence and extreme blood shed will leave the earth full of dead bodies. Goddess of revenge will descend on earth with Caesar’s spirit and the stench of dead bodies will fill the earth.
final_answer: Thus, Antony foresees chaos and destruction in Rome following Caesar's assassination.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of foreshadowing and thematic elements.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What reasons does Brutus give for murdering Caesar?
answer_text: Brutus tells that he killed Caesar because he had become ambitious and wanted to be the king of Rome. He killed Caesar for the betterment of Rome. He was also ready to lay down his life for his country. He honoured Caesar as long as he was heroic but when he became ambitious he killed him.
final_answer: Therefore, Brutus justifies his actions as being in the interest of Rome.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of moral justification and character motivations.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Who says, "Let him be Caesar"? What light does this throw on the speaker?
answer_text: The third citizen says "Let him be Caesar" after Brutus has finished his speech justifying Caesar’s killing. Brutus in his speech proclaims that the public can kill him if he too becomes ambitious like Caesar. He has the same dagger for himself and he is willing to lay down his life for his country. The citizens are fully satisfied. They praise Brutus and show their sympathy for the act.
final_answer: Thus, the statement reflects the citizens' acceptance of Brutus's justification for Caesar's assassination.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character motivations and public sentiment.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Why is Antony's speech more effective?
answer_text: Antony's speech is more effective because it is genuine and full of emotions and feelings for Caesar. He very cleverly tells the crowd that Caesar was not ambitious rather he had refused the crown thrice. He enhanced the glory of Rome with his victories. He left 75 drachmas in his will to be given to every Roman. He left his gardens and property for the common use of the people. He tries to gain the sympathy of the people by showing Caesar’s wounded body. The mob is filled with anger after Antony’s speech and they rush to kill the conspirators.
final_answer: Therefore, Antony's emotional appeal and clever rhetoric incite the crowd against the conspirators.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves analysis of rhetorical techniques and emotional impact.

subject: english_literature
question_text: At the end of the scene what is the fate of Brutus and Cassius?
answer_text: After Antony’s speech, the mob is filled with anger. They rush to kill the conspirators. They burn their houses. Cassius and Brutus plan to face the enemy and discuss their strategy inside a tent. However, both start to quarrel violently but soon become friends. Cassius cannot handle defeat and commits suicide. The ghost of Caesar haunts Brutus. Brutus knows his end is near. He asks Starto to hold his sword, runs on it and dies.
final_answer: Thus, both Brutus and Cassius meet tragic ends due to their involvement in the conspiracy.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding of character arcs and tragic outcomes.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What was Cassius' motive for murdering Julius Caesar?
answer_text: Cassius was jealous of Caesar’s growing power and influence. In fact he didn’t wish to see him as the great conqueror of the world. He didn’t want that Caesar should rule the Romans and that is why he wished to murder him.
final_answer: Cassius' motive was driven by jealousy and the desire for power.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding character motivations and themes of jealousy.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Why was it essential for the conspirators to include Brutus in the conspiracy?
answer_text: It was essential for the conspirators to give a stamp of legitimacy to their cause of murdering Caesar. Brutus was a man of noble ideas. Also he was very close to Caesar. But he fell to the dirty tricks of the conspirators to join them to kill Caesar.
final_answer: Brutus' involvement was crucial for the conspirators' credibility.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character relationships and motivations.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What were the mistakes made by Brutus that led to the failure of the conspiracy?
answer_text: Brutus allowed Antony to give Caesar a suitable funeral after giving a speech to the people at the Capitol. Second, his utter simplicity and belief in Antony. Third, leaving Antony alone with Caesar's dead body and mob. Fourth, his not heeding Cassius's fears in allowing Antony to speak to the people.
final_answer: These mistakes ultimately led to the failure of the conspiracy.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves analysis of multiple actions and their consequences.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Comment on Caesar's friendship with Antony.
answer_text: Antony was a dear friend of Caesar. He did not agree with Brutus that Caesar was an ambitious person who wanted to rule over Rome. In fact he was ready to lay down his life for Rome. After Brutus’ speech at Caesar’s funeral, Antony delivers an emotional speech. He tells the mob that Caesar was not at all ambitious. He refused the crown three times. He said that Caesar had left 75 drachmas for every Roman. Antony appealed to the sentiments of the mob and even showed the wounded corpse of Caesar. The mob was so influenced by Antony’s speech that they turned against the conspirators. Thus Antony showed his affection and respect for Caesar.
final_answer: Antony's actions demonstrate his deep friendship and loyalty to Caesar.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character relationships and emotional appeals.

subject: english_literature
question_text: Write a brief character sketch of Antony.
answer_text: Antony is a noble personality. He has all the human virtues of love, sympathy, sincerity, integrity, solidarity, devotion etc. He is also a great orator and craftsman. He is extremely devoted to Caesar. He wishes that Caesar should be crowned the king. A clever man, Antony, is successful in fooling Brutus into believing that he is with the conspirators after the death of Caesar. He delivers an influential speech which makes the mob realize the conspiracy behind Caesar’s murder. He has genuine love and affection for Caesar and wishes to avenge his death. It is because of his speech, the conspirators are crushed.
final_answer: Antony's character is marked by loyalty, intelligence, and oratory skills.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves synthesis of character traits and their implications.

subject: english_literature
question_text: What is the role of Julius Caesar's ghost in the play, Julius Caesar?
answer_text: The ghost of Julius Caesar appears twice in the play: once before Brutus when he is sleeping in his tent, it stood by his bed side and said nothing. The second time it appears in a battle at Philippi. The ghost appeared in front of Antonius and Octavius. It did not say anything. The purpose of the ghost was to make Brutus realize his mistake. He was carried away by emotions and joined hands with the conspirators. Caesar’s death led to turmoil and unrest in Rome. Brutus is unhappy seeing all this and kills himself with his own sword.
final_answer: Thus, the ghost serves as a reminder of Brutus' guilt and the consequences of his actions.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of character motivations and themes in the play.

subject: english_literature
question_text: How do Brutus and Cassius meet their end?
answer_text: Brutus wants that their forces should move to Philippi and attack the enemy. Cassius does not agree and leaves alone. On the plains of Philippi, Brutus and Cassius reach with their forces where there are the armies of Octavius and Antony. With the interference of Octavius their wrongdoing comes to an end. Then the forces of Cassius and Antony fight in which Antony emerges victorious. Cassius could not accept this defeat and commits suicide. Brutus too is disheartened and kills himself with his own sword.
final_answer: Both Brutus and Cassius ultimately take their own lives after facing defeat.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding the plot and character decisions leading to their demise.
